text_blocks.snippet: The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) includes a methane fee, also known as the "waste emissions charge," that applies to methane emissions above a certain threshold from certain facilities. This fee is intended to encourage reductions in methane emissions, a potent greenhouse gas, from the oil and natural gas sector. The fee is calculated based on the amount of methane emitted and escalates over time, starting at $900 per metric ton in 2024 and increasing to $1,500 per metric ton in 2026 and beyond, according to the CCL Community and the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School.
snippet_highlighted_words: starting at $900 per metric ton in 2024 and increasing to $1,500 per metric ton in 2026 and beyond

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a breakdown of the methane fee:

list.title: Applicability:
list.snippet: The fee applies to facilities within specific industry segments that emit more than 25,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, according to Vinson & Elkins LLP.

list.title: Fee Calculation:
list.snippet: The fee is calculated by multiplying the amount of methane emitted (in metric tons) by the per-ton fee amount, which increases over time.

list.title: Implementation:
list.snippet: The EPA was tasked with implementing the fee, and proposed rules to this effect.

list.title: Congressional Action:
list.snippet: In early 2025, Congress disapproved the EPA's final rule implementing the waste emissions charge using a joint resolution under the Congressional Review Act.

list.title: Current Status:
list.snippet: Following Congressional disapproval, the EPA removed the waste emissions charge regulations from the Code of Federal Regulations.

list.title: Ongoing Evaluation:
list.snippet: The EPA is currently evaluating options and obligations for implementing Clean Air Act section 136(c-g).
